**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental‑health clinician.** I’m glad you’re here today, and I want to thank you for taking a moment for yourself and your well‑being.  

We’re going to complete a short, validated screening tool called the **EPDS** (the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s designed to help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week as you adjust to life with your new baby. The questions are about your emotions, thoughts, and everyday experiences—not about your baby’s health or your parenting skills.

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe, supportive space. My goal is simply to listen and learn what you’re experiencing, so we can determine together what, if any, next steps might be helpful for you.

The EPDS consists of **10 brief questions**. I’ll ask them one at a time, and you can answer in the words that feel most true for you. There are no right or wrong answers—just honest reflections on how you’ve felt during the last seven days.

If at any point a question feels uncomfortable, please let me know, and we can pause or discuss it further.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past week, how often have you felt able to enjoy things the way you used to?*
I’ve definitely not been enjoying things as much as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve hardly ever been able to laugh or see the funny side of things lately.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’m not really looking forward to anything these days. Most of the time I just get through the day without feeling any excitement or anticipation.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Yes, I do find myself blaming myself a lot when things don’t go the way I hoped. I feel guilty and think I’m not doing enough as a mother, even when I’m trying my best.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious a lot lately—worrying about my baby’s health and safety even when there’s no clear reason. The worries keep popping up and it’s hard to shake them, even after I try to calm myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, I’ve had moments where I felt scared or even panicky for no obvious reason—just a sudden rush of fear that something might happen to my baby or that I’m not handling things right. It’s hard to predict when it will hit, but it’s been happening several times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, everything feels like it’s piling up. I’m constantly tired from taking care of the baby, and the worries keep building until I feel overwhelmed. Some days I can manage the basics, but I’m often on edge, crying when the stress gets too much, and I keep telling myself I’m not doing enough. It just feels like it’s all too much to handle.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been having a lot of trouble sleeping. Most nights I either can’t fall asleep at all or I wake up several times and can’t get back to sleep. It feels like I’m tossing and turning for hours, and when I finally do manage a few hours, I wake up feeling exhausted and still worried about the baby. It’s left me feeling drained and more irritable during the day.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve felt really sad and miserable most days this past week. It’s like a heaviness that sits over me, and even when I’m with my baby I can’t shake the feeling that I’m not good enough or that things will never get better. The sadness hangs around and makes everything feel harder than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, I’ve been crying a few times this week—usually when I feel especially stressed or overwhelmed. It often starts with a small thing, like a diaper change that doesn’t go right, and then the tears just come, and I can’t seem to stop them until I’m able to sit down and take a few deep breaths. It leaves me feeling even more exhausted afterward.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts of harming myself.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you - the loss of joy, constant worries, heavy sadness, sleepless nights, and feeling like you're not doing enough as a mother. It's understandable to feel exhausted and tearful when everything feels piled up, and I want you to know you're not alone in these struggles.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports hardly ever able to laugh or see the funny side, matching the 'Not at all' option</sym>, <sym>The patient reports not looking forward to anything and lacking excitement, matching the 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports frequent self-blame, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The mother describes frequent, persistent anxiety and worry without clear reason, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelming stress and inability to cope, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, nightly difficulty sleeping, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, which aligns with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying a few times this week, matching 'Only occasionally</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 23 exceeds the threshold of 14, indicating probable postpartum depression and the need for urgent referral. The patient reports frequent <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>hardly ever able to laugh</quote>), <sym>persistent sadness</sym> (<quote>felt really sad and miserable most days</quote>), intense <sym>guilt</sym> and self‑blame, ongoing <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, frequent <sym>crying</sym>, and high levels of <sym>anxiety</sym> and panic. These symptoms align with DSM‑5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset, which require at least five depressive symptoms, including depressed mood or loss of interest, present most days for at least two weeks, causing functional impairment. Although the screening window is one week, the severity and breadth of symptoms suggest a high likelihood of meeting diagnostic criteria. No suicidal ideation was reported, but continued monitoring is essential. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med>
2. Refer to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive assessment and possible treatment
3. Provide information about local postpartum support groups and peer networks
4. Encourage sleep hygiene practices such as establishing a consistent bedtime routine and seeking help with nighttime infant care
5. Discuss a safety plan and monitor for any emergence of suicidal thoughts or self‑harm urges
6. Offer brief psychoeducation about postpartum anxiety and depression and coping strategies
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Post‑partum Mental Health Screening Summary**

**Client ID / Date:** ______________________  

**Screening Tool:** Structured symptom interview (post‑partum mood & anxiety)

| **Domain** | **Client Report** | **Screening Significance** |
|------------|-------------------|----------------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low Positive Affect** | “Hardly ever able to laugh or see the funny side of things.”; “Not really looking forward to anything; no excitement or anticipation.” | Consistent loss of pleasure and diminished interest – core features of depressive symptomatology. |
| **Sad Mood** | Persistent sadness and “miserable” feeling most days; heaviness that does not lift even when with baby. | Persistent low mood – primary depressive indicator. |
| **Crying / Tearfulness** | Crying several times per week, triggered by minor stressors, difficulty stopping. | Emotional dysregulation and depressive symptom severity. |
| **Sleep Disturbance** | Trouble falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings, non‑restorative sleep, daytime exhaustion. | Sleep disruption is both a symptom and a maintaining factor for mood disturbance. |
| **Guilt / Self‑blame** | Frequent self‑blame, feeling “not doing enough as a mother,” pervasive guilt. | Cognitive pattern of worthlessness/guilt common in postpartum depression. |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Excessive, intrusive worries about baby’s health and safety without clear trigger; feels anxious “a lot.” | Heightened anxiety; may reflect comorbid postpartum anxiety. |
| **Panic / Fear** | Sudden, unexplained panic or fear that something will happen to baby or that she is not handling things correctly. | Panic‑type symptoms increase overall distress and functional impairment. |
| **Overwhelm / Stress** | “Everything feels like it’s piling up,” feeling “on edge,” frequent crying when stress escalates. | Indicates difficulty coping and possible burnout. |
| **Suicidal Ideation** | Denies any thoughts of self‑harm. | No immediate safety concern reported. |

**Pattern Summary**  
- The client exhibits a coherent cluster of depressive symptoms (anhedonia, persistent low mood, tearfulness, sleep disturbance, guilt) together with significant anxiety manifestations (excessive worry, panic/fear, feeling overwhelmed).  
- Symptoms are reported as occurring most days over the past week and appear to interfere with daily functioning (sleep, emotional regulation, caregiving).  

**Risk Factors Identified**  
- Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure.  
- Frequent crying spells.  
- Marked sleep disruption.  
- Prominent feelings of guilt and self‑blame.  
- High anxiety and panic symptoms.  
- No reported suicidal ideation or self‑harm thoughts at this time.  

**Safety/Follow‑up Considerations**  
- Continue to monitor for emergence of suicidal thoughts or self‑harm behaviors.  
- Given the severity and breadth of depressive and anxiety symptoms, a formal diagnostic evaluation and referral for comprehensive perinatal mental‑health assessment is warranted.  

**Clinician Signature:** ______________________   **Date:** _______________   **Credentials:** ______________________
